title: Who gets to decide what school improvement means?
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes uses Matthew McCluskey's paper on the school improvement industry to ask who defines improvement in schools. She accepts that schools need outside challenge and expertise, but argues that the trouble starts when external support becomes external authority and fragmented consultants, trusts and providers define, package and sell change. Scripted curricula, behaviour packages and PD programmes can help, yet they can also reduce teacher judgement to compliance and turn teachers into consumers of other people's models. She treats teacher resistance as a possible source of knowledge rather than a nuisance and separates buying improvement from building capacity, which is slower but stays when the provider leaves. Her test for any programme is whether teachers become more expert, and she closes with a list of questions leaders should ask before adopting one.
points: External support becomes a problem when it becomes external authority, with providers defining the problem, brokering the evidence and selling the solution.
Fidelity, coherence and consistency can become code for reduced teacher judgement, and resistance can be intelligent because teachers know pupils, timetable and context that a model cannot.
Buying improvement is efficient but leaves nothing behind; building capacity through teacher-led curriculum work and department inquiry is slower but remains when the provider leaves.
The test of any programme is whether teachers become more expert, and a programme that mainly gives leaders something to monitor is probably not improvement.
She offers seven questions for leaders, including who designed this, whose evidence is used, and what knowledge will remain once the programme ends.
quotes: The problem is not external support. Schools need outside eyes, challenge and expertise. The problem comes when support arrives in fragments, each piece asking for attention, each expert naming a slightly different version of the problem, and nobody staying long enough to build the capacity of the people who will still be there on Monday morning.

McCluskey argues that, over the last 25 years, educational change has increasingly shifted away from educators and towards private organisations, intermediary bodies, philanthropic networks and reform providers. These groups do not merely support change. Increasingly, they define it, package it, sell it, broker evidence for it, and position themselves as the people with answers.

The uncomfortable truth is that “evidence-informed” can be used badly. Evidence does not speak for itself. It is selected, framed, simplified and marketed. A provider may not be lying, but it will still tell a story in which its solution appears necessary. The school improvement industry does not only offer products; it offers narratives. Here is the problem. Here is the proof. Here is the solution. Here is the implementation route. Here is the training. Here is the dashboard. Here is the invoice.
But resistance can also be intelligent. Sometimes teachers resist because they can see what the model cannot. They know the pupils. They know the subject.

Building capacity is slower. It asks teachers to read, plan, test, discuss, adapt, observe, disagree, refine and own the work. It requires time. It requires trust. It requires leaders to tolerate some mess.

It means teachers should be on the leading edge of change, not at the sharp end of implementation. It means external expertise should serve professional judgement, not replace it. It means teachers should be treated as knowledge-workers, not end-users.
